title: A Guide to Using spacyr
text: spacyr provides convenient R wrapper around Python spaCy package. offers easy access following functionality spaCy: parsing texts tokens sentences; lemmatizing tokens; parsing dependencies (identify grammatical structure sentence); identifying, extracting, consolidating token sequences form named entities noun phrases. also allows user request additional token-level attributes directly spaCy. spacyr also takes care installation spaCy also Python , self-contained virtual environment, can install additional language models upgrade spaCy new models versions become available. Finally, spacyr works seamlessly quanteda package, although use optional.

title: A Guide to Using spacyr
text: spacyr works reticulate package allows R harness power Python. access underlying Python functionality, spacyr must open connection initialized within R session. provide function , spacy_initialize(), attempts make process painless possible. spaCy installed spacy_install() (see https://spacyr.quanteda.io detailed instructions), spacy_initialize() uses virtual environment created. spacy_installed() checks whether environment, language models need, ready. Users setup spaCy, instance conda environment, can instead point spacyr Python executable environment setting RETICULATE_PYTHON environment variable calling spacy_initialize(), e.g. Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = reticulate::conda_python("-spacy-env")).
code: library("spacyr") spacy_initialize(model = "en_core_web_sm") ## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)

title: A Guide to Using spacyr
text: spacy_parse() function spacyr’s main workhorse. calls spaCy tokenize tag texts. provides two options part speech tagging, plus options return word lemmas, recognize names entities noun phrases recognition, identify grammatical structures features parsing syntactic dependencies. returns data.frame corresponding emerging text interchange format token data.frames. tokenization approach taken spaCy inclusive: includes tokens without restrictions, including punctuation characters symbols. Example: Two fields available part--speech tags. pos field returned Universal tagset parts--speech, general scheme users find serves needs, also provides equivalencies across languages. spacyr also provides detailed tagset, defined spaCy language model. English, OntoNotes 5 version Penn Treebank tag set. Penn Treebank specific English parts speech. language models, detailed tagset based different scheme. German language model, instance, universal tagset (pos) remains , detailed tagset (tag) based TIGER Treebank scheme. model’s tags listed “Label scheme” spaCy models web page. Direct parsing texts also possible, using spacy_tokenize(). options designed match tokens() function quanteda package. default returns named list (document name list element name): can also output data.frame:
code: txt <- c(d1 = "spaCy is great at fast natural language processing.",          d2 = "Mr. Smith spent two years in North Carolina.")  # process documents and obtain a data.table parsedtxt <- spacy_parse(txt) parsedtxt ##    doc_id sentence_id token_id      token      lemma   pos   entity ## 1      d1           1        1      spaCy      spacy   NUM          ## 2      d1           1        2         is         be   AUX          ## 3      d1           1        3      great      great   ADJ          ## 4      d1           1        4         at         at   ADP          ## 5      d1           1        5       fast       fast   ADJ          ## 6      d1           1        6    natural    natural   ADJ          ## 7      d1           1        7   language   language  NOUN          ## 8      d1           1        8 processing processing  NOUN          ## 9      d1           1        9          .          . title: A Guide to Using spacyr
text: spacyr can extract entities, either named “extended” output spacy_parse(). “Extended” entities including entities dates, events, cardinal ordinal quantities. One useful feature use consolidation functions compound multi-word entities single “tokens” (language like German): similar manner named entity extraction, spacyr can extract concatenate [noun phrases* (noun chunks). Just entities, noun phrases can also consolidated single “tokens”: user’s goal entity noun phrase extraction, two functions make easy without first parsing entire text:

title: A Guide to Using spacyr
text: default, spacyr loads English language model. also can load spaCy’s language models giving model’s full name, path model directory, model option spacy_initialize(). spacyr requires spaCy 3.0.0 later, short model names spaCy 2, "en" "de", longer work. small models languages : example parsing German texts. Note additional language models must first installed spaCy. spaCy installed spacy_install(), installation additional language models simple. example, German language model can installed (spacy_download_langmodel("de_core_news_sm")). environments, can install model entering python -m spacy download de_core_news_sm console.
code: ## first finalize the old instance of spaCy if it's loaded spacy_finalize() spacy_initialize(model = "de_core_news_sm") ## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: de_core_news_sm)  txt_german <- c(R = "R ist eine freie Programmiersprache für statistische Berechnungen und Grafiken. Sie wurde von Statistikern für Anwender mit statistischen Aufgaben entwickelt.",                python = "Python ist eine universelle, üblicherweise interpretierte höhere Programmiersprache. Sie will einen gut lesbaren, knappen Programmierstil fördern.") results_german <- spacy_parse(txt_german, dependency = FALSE, lemma = FALSE, tag = TRUE) results_german ##    doc_id sentence_id token_id              token   pos   tag entity ## 1       R           1        1                  R     X    XY        ## 2       R           1        2                ist   AUX VAFIN        ## 3       R           1        3               eine   DET   ART        ## 4       R           1        4              freie   ADJ  ADJA        ## 5       R           1        5 Programmiersprache  NOUN    NN        ## 6       R           1        6                für   ADP  APPR        ## 7       R           1        7       statistische   ADJ  ADJA        ## 8       R           1        8       Berechnungen  NOUN    NN        ## 9       R           1        9                und CCONJ   KON        ## 10      R           1       10           Grafiken  NOUN    NN        ## 11      R           1       11                  . Conversion tokens easily performed, tokenizers spacyr tend smarter purely syntactic pattern-based parsers used quanteda. latter useful say, selecting nouns, using “glob” pattern matching quanteda’s tokens_select() function: Direct conversion just spaCy-based tokens also possible: including sentences, spaCy’s recognition smart: also works well entity recognition, e.g.
code: require(quanteda, warn.conflicts = FALSE, quietly = TRUE) docnames(parsedtxt) ## [1] "d1" "d2" ndoc(parsedtxt) ## [1] 2 ntoken(parsedtxt) ## d1 d2  ##  9  9 ntype(parsedtxt) ## d1 d2  ##  9  9 spacy_initialize(model = "en_core_web_sm") ## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm) parsedtxt <- spacy_parse(txt, pos = TRUE, tag = TRUE) as.tokens(parsedtxt) ## tokens of 2 documents (18 tokens, 17 types). ## d1 : ## [1] "spaCy"      "is"         "great"      "at"         "fast"       ## [6] "natural"    "language"   "processing" "."          ##  ## d2 : ## [1] "Mr."      "Smith"    "spent"    "two"      "years"    "in"       "North"    ## [8] "Carolina" "." as.tokens(parsedtxt, include_pos = "pos") ## tokens of 2 documents (18 tokens, 17 types). ## d1 : ## [1] "spaCy/NUM"       "is/AUX"          "great/ADJ"       "at/ADP"          ## [5] "fast/ADJ"        "natural/ADJ"     "language/NOUN"   "processing/NOUN" ## [9] "./PUNCT"         ##  ## d2 : ## [1] "Mr./PROPN"      "Smith/PROPN"    "spent/VERB"     "two/NUM"        ## [5] "years/NOUN"     "in/ADP"         "North/PROPN"    "Carolina/PROPN" ## [9] "./PUNCT" as.tokens(parsedtxt, include_pos = "tag") ## tokens of 2 documents (18 tokens, 17 types). ## d1 : ## [1] "spaCy/CD"      "is/VBZ"        "great/JJ"      "at/IN"         ## [5] "fast/JJ"       "natural/JJ"    "language/NN"   "processing/NN" ## [9] "./."           ##  ## d2 : ## [1] "Mr./NNP"      "Smith/NNP"    "spent/VBD"    "two/CD"       "years/NNS"    ## [6] "in/IN"        "North/NNP"    "Carolina/NNP" "./." spacy_parse("The cat in the hat ate green eggs and ham.", pos = TRUE) %>%     as.tokens(include_pos = "pos") %>%     tokens_select(pattern = c("*/NOUN")) ## tokens of 1 document (4 tokens, 4 types). ## text1 : ## [1] "cat/NOUN"  "hat/NOUN"  "eggs/NOUN" "ham/NOUN" spacy_tokenize(txt) %>%     as.tokens() ## tokens of 2 documents (18 tokens, 17 types). ## d1 : ## [1] "spaCy"      "is"         "great"      "at"         "fast"       ## [6] "natural"    "language"   "processing" "."          ##  ## d2 : ## [1] "Mr."      "Smith"    "spent"    "two"      "years"    "in"       "North"    ## [8] "Carolina" "." txt2 <- "A Ph.D. in Washington D.C.  Mr. Smith went to Washington." spacy_tokenize(txt2, what = "sentence") %>%     as.tokens() ## tokens of 1 document (1 token, 1 type). ## text1 : ## [1] "A Ph.D. in Washington D.C.  Mr. Smith went to Washington." spacy_parse(txt, entity = TRUE) %>%     entity_consolidate() %>%     as.tokens() %>%      head(1) ## tokens of 1 document (9 tokens, 15 types). ## d1 : ## [1] "spaCy"      "is"         "great"      "at"         "fast"       ## [6] "natural"    "language"   "processing" "."
